papers.title: Optimization of synchronizability and shortest-path length in evolving spatial networks
papers.authors: Paula Rodríguez-Sánchez, Johann H. Martínez, Javier Martín Buldú
papers.abstract: Spatial networks are constrained by both topology and geometry, and these constraints may affect their capacity to support efficient communication and stable collective dynamics. Here, we study how the spatial position of nodes can be used as an optimization parameter in networks with fixed topology and distance-dependent weights. Starting from spatially embedded Barabási–Albert networks, we apply a simulated annealing relocation algorithm and compare different optimization criteria based on the Laplacian eigenratio Q = λ N / λ 2 , the average shortest-path length d , the combined objective Q × d , λ 2 , and λ 2 / d . We show that minimizing d alone produces highly centralized spatial configurations that shorten paths but increase λ N and therefore impair synchronizability. Conversely, minimizing Q promotes more homogeneous centrality patterns, improving spectral synchronizability but leaving the path length practically unchanged. The combined optimization of Q × d generates a compromise configuration that reduces shortest paths while preserving a favorable Laplacian spectrum. Spatial descriptors based on entropy, Voronoi-cell variability, wiring length and outreach reveal that each optimization strategy leaves a distinct geometric signature. Finally, simulations of Hindmarsh–Rose neurons and a Master Stability Function analysis indicate that the dynamical benefit of spatial optimization depends strongly on network density: sparse Barabási–Albert networks remain difficult to synchronize, whereas denser Erdős–Rényi networks exhibit lower synchronization error after optimization. These results extend the idea of entangled networks to spatially embedded systems and show that functional improvements can emerge from geometry alone, even when topology is kept fixed.

papers.title: Network Motifs: Simple Building Blocks of Complex Networks
papers.authors: R. Milo, S. Shen-Orr, S. Itzkovitz, N. Kashtan, D. Chklovskii, U. Alon
papers.abstract: Complex networks are studied across many fields of science. To uncover their structural design principles, we defined “network motifs,” patterns of interconnections occurring in complex networks at numbers that are significantly higher than those in randomized networks. We found such motifs in networks from biochemistry, neurobiology, ecology, and engineering. The motifs shared by ecological food webs were distinct from the motifs shared by the genetic networks of Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae or from those found in the World Wide Web. Similar motifs were found in networks that perform information processing, even though they describe elements as different as biomolecules within a cell and synaptic connections between neurons in Caenorhabditis elegans . Motifs may thus define universal classes of networks. This approach may uncover the basic building blocks of most networks.
